title: Ramadan: the night prayers
hook: long night prayers in the mosque, the whole Qur'an recited over the month

segments.voice: Yesterday: iftar, breaking the fast with a date and water, the first of two joys. Your line was sweet at sunset. Did you start your evening with something small and sweet? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Ten at night in Ramadan, and the mosque parking lot is fuller than on a Friday. Inside, rows and rows of people, shoulder to shoulder, standing. At the front, one voice is reciting, and it keeps going, page after page, clear and long. Kids fall asleep on the carpet at the back. A grandmother sits on a chair by the wall. The standing lasts an hour, sometimes more. And by the last night of the month, if you'd come every night, you'd have heard the whole Qur'an, cover to cover. Today: the night prayers.
screen: `TEN AT NIGHT, A FULL PARKING LOT.` → `ONE VOICE, PAGE AFTER PAGE.` → `COVER TO COVER BY MONTH'S END.`

segments.voice: These prayers are called tarawih, from a word for rest, because the people who prayed them long ago would sit and rest after every four units. The prayer is voluntary, not one of the five, but in Ramadan it has a special place. A hadith in Bukhari says: whoever stands in prayer in Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward, their past sins are forgiven. And here's the story of how it began. Aisha said that one Ramadan the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night in the mosque, and some people prayed behind him. The next night more came. The next, more still. Then one night, the mosque was full, and he didn't come out. In the morning he explained: I saw what you were doing, and nothing kept me away except that I feared it would be made obligatory on you. He didn't want to turn a gift into a burden. Years later, the second caliph, Umar, walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying in scattered little groups, each behind a different reciter. So he gathered them behind one reciter, a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b. And the next night, seeing them all together, he said: what a fine new thing this is. How many units? Communities differ, openly. Some pray eight, following a report from Aisha. Many pray twenty, as in the great mosque in Mecca. Many Shia Muslims pray the extra night prayers of Ramadan on their own, not in congregation. But everywhere, the idea is the same. The days of Ramadan are for fasting. The nights are for standing.
screen: `TARAWIH — FROM A WORD FOR REST.` · `STAND IN RAMADAN, OUT OF FAITH.` · `HE FEARED IT WOULD BE MADE A DUTY.` · `UMAR GATHERED THEM BEHIND ONE.` · then, large: `EIGHT, OR TWENTY, OR ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand a little longer tonight. Before bed, stand still for a minute or two, feet planted, hands folded or at your sides. If you pray, add two voluntary rak'ahs tonight, or make one standing a little longer than usual, reciting slowly. If you don't, just stand in a quiet room, and listen to the house at night. Notice how different the night feels from the day. When your legs start to ask to sit, stay one breath longer. The bell holds the time.
Tarawih. The long night prayers of Ramadan, named for the rests between them, the Qur'an recited over the month. Today's word.
Your line: the nights are for standing. Tonight, give the last ten minutes before sleep to something quiet, instead of a screen. Day one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: During Ramadan, many Sunni Muslims gather after the night prayer for tarawih, eight or twenty rak'ahs led by a reciter who often completes the whole Qur'an over the month; many Shia Muslims pray extra Ramadan night prayers individually.

gather them all behind one reciter

original.note: Arabic: the Ramadan night prayers, from a word for rest, for the pauses after every four units.

trapdoor: what you thought: tarawih is an extra prayer at the mosque in Ramadan.
what it means: long voluntary night prayers, named for their rests, where the whole Qur'an is often heard over the month.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 2012 (he feared it becoming obligatory), Umar's 'fine innovation' (Bukhari 2010), and the eight-or-twenty debate.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 37 (whoever stands in Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2012 (the Prophet did not come out, fearing it would be made obligatory)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2010 (Umar gathers the people behind Ubayy ibn Ka'b)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1147 (Aisha: he did not exceed eleven rak'ahs, in Ramadan or otherwise)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.

Umar's phrase (ni'mat al-bid'ah hadhihi) is rendered 'what a fine new thing this is'; the word bid'ah is sensitive and scholars interpret it in its linguistic sense. A Keeper may prefer different wording.

Shia view: congregational tarawih is not practiced, and many Shia scholars regard its congregational form as not established by the Prophet; the script says only that many Shia pray extra Ramadan night prayers individually. Please review for balance.
Eight rak'ahs following Aisha's report (eleven with witr); twenty as in Mecca and the majority of the four Sunni schools historically.
